claims.notes: A PUBLIC MEETING CALLED AT A NAMED CHICAGO PUBLIC HOUSE. 'The Eagle Hotel, (Steele's)' is the house identified by its keeper, which is how this town names its taverns; the gazetteer already carries an Eagle Hotel from July 1834 under P. B. F. Cable and from October under J. Shrigley, so Steele is an EARLIER keeper of the same sign, five months before Cable. Whether the sign moved houses is not said and is not inferred. The town is meeting to send a delegate to a county convention at Ottawa, LaSalle county, and the notice reaches out to Hickory Creek, Naper's Settlement and Walker's Grove — the settlements this town's district then ran to.

claims.notes: A BUILDING SOLD AT AUCTION, AND THE PAPER PLACES IT BY A BRIDGE — 'the Building formerly occupied as the Meeting House, opposite the bridge over the North Branch of the Chicago river'. Three things a reconstruction can use and one it cannot. It can use: a bridge stood over the NORTH Branch on 6 February 1834 and was a landmark specific enough to place a building by; a building stood across the street from it; and that building had been the town's meeting house — the room the Presbyterians used before the church T-0310 read dedicated on 1834-01-21. It CANNOT use it for a footprint, a size or a material: the notice gives none, and none is supplied. The two platted parcels in the same sale — West half of Lot 3 in Block 44, and Lot 7 in Block 8 — are quoted as printed and are NOT resolved against the plat here; that is a placement question and this is a reading pass.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S OWN GOVERNMENT SPECIFYING ITS TWO BRIDGES, AND THIS IS THE MOST BUILDABLE THING IN THE MONTH. Both branch bridges existed in February 1834 and both needed repair; the south bridge needed A NEW BENT, which says it was a trestle carried on bents and not a float. The scantling is printed and is the only period dimensioning of these structures this corpus holds: braces of oak timber 6 inches square, oak railing 8 by 4 inches for both bridges, oak standards for the railing 4 feet high, oak plank 2 inches thick for the flooring, the flooring pinned down with oak pins 1 1/2 inches in diameter and 2 feet long, the railing secured by spikes or pins. WHAT IS CUT AND NOT SUPPLIED: the number of braces, the standards' spacing, and the bridges' spans and widths — the column's left edge takes all four, and a dimension guessed at here would be a dimension built. The signature is the Trustees', which dates the town's corporate maintenance of the crossings to 4 January 1834.

claims.notes: THE EARLIEST ADDRESS THIS CORPUS HOLDS FOR COLLINS & CATON, and it is not the one the gazetteer had. The firm's July 1834 advertisement places the office 'two doors east of the Baptist Church, fitted up stairs, South Water-street' (1834-07-02, claim c016 there); five months earlier it is placed off a MERCHANT instead — one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co. — on the same street. Both anchors are the paper's own and neither is corrected by the other; taken together they say Brewster, Hogan & Co. and the Baptist Church stood within a few doors of each other on South Water Street, which is a relation a placement pass can use and this pass does not spend. The word 'one' before 'door' is cut in this printing and is supplied from the identical standing advertisement in the next two issues (1834-02-18 page 3 column 4 line 2525, 1834-02-25 page 3 column 4 line 2498), which both read 'NE door cast of' for 'ONE door east of'.

claims.notes: THE SHOP THE GAZETTEER ALREADY CARRIED, NOW WITH ITS PROPRIETORS. The same standing advertisement was read on 1834-01-07 (claim c007 there) off a transcription that lost the firm's name, and the business went into the gazetteer anonymously as 'the new blacksmith shop opposite the Chicago Hotel' with an empty proprietors list. It is PIERCE & ABBOTT, printed clearly here and again on 1834-02-11 (line 2341) and 1834-02-18 (line 2529). The entry is deliberately claimed under the SAME business name so the two readings compile into one business rather than two; the anonymous name stays because it is the gazetteer's key, and this claim is what puts the men in it. THE SHOP ALSO MAKES PRAIRIE PLOUGHS TO ORDER, which is a manufacture and not only a smithy.

claims.notes: WHAT IT COST TO BUILD IN CHICAGO IN FEBRUARY 1834, in the paper's own weekly table, under its own heading 'Building Materials'. Poplar lumber assorted at $20-23 the thousand feet, shingles $3.50-4.00, square timber by the running foot, lath $6.00 the thousand, lime by the perch, hair by the barrel and sand by the cord: a costing for the exact materials the buildings in this reconstruction are made of, three weeks before the schooners can bring any more. THE FIGURES ARE READ OFF A DAMAGED COLUMN and the item names are cut at the left edge; each is supplied inside brackets from the row's own units, which is the only thing that constrains them, and a reader who wants them beyond doubt should go to the page image. The lines quoted are the heading and the building-materials block only; the flour, provision, dry-goods and exchange blocks between them are not claimed here. P. F. Peck reports the table and is the same P. F. W. Peck whose store stands at the corner of LaSalle and South Water — the town's price current is compiled by one of its merchants.

claims.notes:
THE JANUARY 1834 CHICAGO LETTER LIST, A THIRD TIME, AND THIS IS THE BEST WITNESS THE CORPUS HAS FOR ITS FIRST HALF. Ruling 1 applies in full: this is Chicago's own post office, so every listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged `letter_list_only`.

WHY IT IS MINTED AGAIN AND NOT RECORDED AS A REPRINT. T-0292's rule is that a list printed more than once is minted ONCE, from the witness that carries it whole, so that one list makes one cohort of people. That rule is kept here rather than broken: this is the SAME list and therefore the SAME cohort, and the gazetteer keys on the normalized name, so a name already minted from 1834-01-28 gains a mention and not a second person. What the minting adds is the names that printing LOST. T-0310 read the January printings out of a `.docx` transcription that crushed the list's two alphabetical columns into eight paragraph lines and left orphan debris where names stood, and recorded its 97 names as a FLOOR; T-0318 was opened to close the gap off the page images, on the finding that 'the two printings do not repair each other and the images are the only route'. THAT FINDING WAS MADE WITHOUT THIS THIRD PRINTING, which is in the ruled dialect, one name to a line, and repairs the A-to-G run without a scan.

THE HAND COUNT THE TICKET ASKS FOR. Counted by eye off the printed list as this transcription preserves it: the left alphabetical run of page 4 column 2 carries SIXTY-TWO personal names on lines 2860-2931, and this claim mints sixty-two, plus the postmaster — sixty-three entities. Two of them stand on one line (2893, 'Lamira& Laura Carrier'). Two further lines inside the range carry a token where a name stands and cannot be read as one (2926 'William      ing 2', 2932); THEY ARE NOT MINTED and are not counted, because a person in the gazetteer under a name nobody can match is the exact cost T-0318 records. The RIGHT-HAND alphabetical run on these same lines is cut to forenames — 'Isanc K', 'Jacob |', 'Mirand' — and mints nobody. The list continues into page 4 column 3, where the initials are cut instead; see claim c014.

WHAT THIS PRINTING REPAIRS, name by name, against the 1834-01-28 reading: it completes 'William Cr[…]' to William Criss, '[?] Devoe' to Samuel Devoe, '[uncertain: Dagenet]' to Noel Dagenet, '[?] Gooding' to Jos. A. Gooding, '[uncertain: Childress]' to James Childress, '[uncertain: D. P. Cleviny]' to D. P. Clevinger, '[uncertain: Orinda Guryl]' to Orinda Gary and 'G. W. Ewin[g]' to G. W. Ewing; and it adds about twenty names the January printing does not carry at all, among them J. W. Anderson, A. Bertrand, Joseph Babou, A. P. Benton, Thomas Conger, Alfred Clarke, Henry B. Clarke, Alfred Churchill, Daniel B. Clevinger, Lamira and Laura Carrier, Loring Delano, P. Field and O. Grant. It also DISAGREES with it twice: 'I. K. Blodgett' is set J. K. Blodgett here, and 'Jane Forster' is set Jane Forrister. Both readings are left standing as each witness prints them.

NO MERGES ARE DECLARED, and that is deliberate. Several of the repairs above are the same person under two spellings, but the gazetteer's own rule bars merging a same-surname pair whose initials differ, and the rest turn on a single damaged letter. Declaring them off two damaged transcriptions would be guessing with a `merge_rule` attached. They are named here instead, and T-0318's pass over the page images is where they should be settled.

Where a February reading is unambiguously the same name the January printing set more fully, the January string is used verbatim (Russell Baldwin for 'Russel', Geo. H. Clark for 'Geo. 1, Clark', E. Dimmick for 'E Dimaiick', David Dickson for 'avi ichson') — the two printings of one list are parallel readings of one setting, which is the transcription workflow's own rule for using them. The dateline is read January 1 from the January printing; this one sets it '1934' for 1834 and the day is damaged.

claims.notes:
THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME LIST, AND IT MINTS NOBODY. Page 4 column 3 carries the H-to-W run of the 1 January 1834 Chicago letter list and the segmenter's crop has taken the left edge off every line, so what survives is seventy-three bare surnames with no forename and no initial: 'Johnson', 'Smith', 'Taylor', 'Wilson 4'. NOT ONE OF THEM IS MINTED. Ruling 1 mints a listed NAME, and a surname with the initial cut away is not one — it is the unmatchable entry T-0318 identifies as the concrete cost of reading this list off a damaged column, and minting seventy-three of them would manufacture that cost at scale. The 1834-01-28 printing carries this half BETTER than this one does (Lewis Kercheval, Salmon Rutherford, S. W. Smith, Isaac Scarritt, Palmer Stearns, Alden Tuller, Elam Tuller, Aaron Whitcomb), which is the mirror of what happens in column 2, where this printing is the better witness. SO THE TWO PRINTINGS DO REPAIR EACH OTHER, in opposite halves — which is the finding T-0318 was opened without. The postmaster's signature closes the list here and is minted in claim c013, where its first half stands.

The lines quoted are the two heading fragments, the seventy-three surname lines, and the signature; the advertisements woven through the same lines from the neighbouring printed column are excluded, which is what `lines_of_claim` names.
